figures.caption: Figure 2. Decoding during free viewing. A, An example eye trace (yellow) of a marmoset viewing a static scene, with V1 receptive fields (RFs). The inset zooms in on fixation 4 to show their scale. The light blue circles are the overlaid RFs of 190 V1 units. The cyan square is the patch the models predict. It sits at a fixed offset from gaze (red dot). B, Spikes of 190 V1 units (rows) and gaze over time. Each jump in gaze is a saccade. Fixations are numbered as in A. The box marks fixation 4 (inset in A). C, The scene decoded from V1 by the diffusion model. The inset shows where V1 RFs landed over all fixations, trials and sessions. Fig. S2 shows the same for macaque LGN.

Figure 3. Ridge-decoded patches and a scene prior. A, Measured gaze (yellow) and receptive-field patch locations (cyan). B, Spikes spanning four fixations, with decoded and true patches; dotted lines mark saccades, and cyan bands mark the 100-ms decoder windows. C, The mosaic is the weighted average of all decoded patches (Eq. 4); the arrow places the decoded patch of fixation 4 from B at its position in C. D, The 1/ f prior denoises and fills in the gaps. Fig. S3 shows the same for macaque LGN.

Figure 4. Transformer decoding and a learned diffusion prior. The decoder, built from a transformer [47] and Stable Diffusion [48]. Each token embeds a 100-ms window of spiking activity and the gaze track, at a 16.7-ms stride. A separate patch head trains the token embeddings to predict each window’s local image patch. The transformer is trained from scratch; its decoded scene and the neural query features condition the diffusion model. Right: a held-out marmoset V1 scene, with its transformer and diffusion reconstructions.

Figure 5. Comparison with published brain decoders. A, The table quantifies each method’s correlation to the original photograph, overall and in different frequency bands. The transformer is the best in every column. B, Example reconstructions decoded from MEG, EEG, fMRI and electrophysiology. Methods are ordered by correlation to the original photograph. V1→IT means V1, V4 and IT arrays. C, Perceptual similarity (LPIPS) versus correlation for selected decoders (all in Fig. S6); lines join our transformer (open) to diffusion (filled), and dashed steps mark the gaps between the best non-invasive, invasive and ex vivo decoders. Numbered as in B.

Figure 6. Neural evidence: viewing time, coverage and neuron count. A, One held-out scene after 10 s to 10 min of viewing. B, Accuracy over viewing time for 27 scenes. Left: the transformer’s correlation with the photograph in three spatial-frequency bands, with 95% bootstrap intervals. Middle and right: every decoder’s correlation and LPIPS. C, The same scene as receptive field coverage increases across columns. Each blue dot in the RF row is a sampled receptive field location. The rows below set the number of neurons at each blue dot. D, Mean correlation over the 27 scenes for C’s grid. Contours show the coverage-neuron trade-off. Fig. S4 shows macaque LGN.
